entries.claim: Reporting real contiguous region extents from NtQueryVirtualMemory (instead of a flat 64KB) fixes the memory-walk hang
entries.evidence:
Replaced the flat 0x10000 RegionSize with the true extents from xbox_memory_layout.h - four regions (low memory, XBE image, 8MB stack, heap to end of RAM) plus a catch-all above 0x04000000 reporting free to the top of the address space. Reasoning was that a 64MB walk in 64KB steps needs ~1000 iterations and never finished, so real extents should take five. Measured, deterministic 2 of 2: kernel_calls COLLAPSED 4000 -> 58, safe_stub 1 -> 8, failed_icalls 1 -> 2, and the crash came back (access violation at RVA 0xD247F0). heap_allocs rose 13 -> 18, so it is doing something different early, not simply dying sooner. Reverted immediately per rule #14; the flat-64KB version restored 4000/1/13/1 with no crash on 2 of 2, so the regression is entirely attributable to this change. NOT YET DIAGNOSED - candidates worth separating before retrying: (a) the ~49MB heap reported as ONE committed region may make the caller believe a huge contiguous block exists and act on it, (b) the above-RAM catch-all computes size as 0xFFFFFFFF - base which is close to overflow and may wrap in the caller's arithmetic, (c) reporting region_base BELOW the queried address (true extents start low, the granule version did not) may break a walker that assumes BaseAddress <= returned base. Do not simply re-apply this whole change; test (b) alone first, it is the cheapest and the most likely to be an outright bug in my code rather than a semantic mismatch.</evidence>

entries.claim: The pool-growth hang is not a retry cycle: it is ONE unbounded address-space sweep that wraps the full 4GB forever, 21.6 million NtQueryVirtualMemory calls, driven by our own flat 64KB RegionSize
entries.evidence: Added a pure-logging counter inside bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory (no [KERNEL] # line, so kernel_calls stays comparable; signals unchanged at 4000/1/13/1 deterministic 2 of 2). Measured: 21,659,648+ NtQueryVirtualMemory calls in one boot and still climbing, with backsteps=335 - the sweep runs off the top of the 32-bit address space and WRAPS to low addresses 335 times. 335 wraps x 65,536 steps/wrap = 21.9M, which matches the call count, so the arithmetic is closed. Consecutive logged addresses differ by exactly 0x10000000 = 4096 x 0x10000, confirming the caller advances by EXACTLY the RegionSize we hand it, one 64KB granule per call. Every single call reports FREE; NtAllocateVirtualMemory is called only TWICE in the whole boot (1MB at base=0, 4KB at 0x00F81000), both early and unrelated - the sweep NEVER results in an allocation attempt. THREE corrections to the record. (1) The "4000 kernel calls" headline is a LOGGING CAP, not the real count - kernel_bridge.c:1821 gates the [KERNEL] # line at 4000 and progress/smoke_spread derive kernel_calls by counting those lines, exactly the failure its own comment warns about. The true count is 5000x higher. (2) sub_0020F0B2 is NOT a retry-loop head; it is a free-list node decoder - it reads a block header at [ebp], unpacks a 19-bit size field (plus 12 high bits when bit31 is set), rounds to 4, and compares the node against the embedded list head at edx+0x48. The 2026-08-05 note calling it the loop head is wrong. (3) Ledger #30's premise was wrong by four orders of magnitude: it assumed "a 64MB walk in 64KB steps needs ~1000 iterations", but the walk is not bounded by RAM at all - it is the full 4GB, wrapping. So the hang is a single non-terminating search, not the sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209 -> sub_0020F0B2 retry cycle described in earlier notes. ROOT CAUSE: we tell the caller that all 4GB above the 64MB of RAM is free memory in 64KB pieces. It is looking for a contiguous run bigger than 64KB, we never report one, so it steps 64KB and asks again, forever. NOT YET TESTED: returning an error status above XBOX_TOTAL_RAM (what real hardware does) instead of a successful FREE region. That is distinct from #30's candidates (a)(b)(c), all of which still report success.

entries.claim: Ledger #30 was not a regression and should not have been reverted: ending the sweep by ANY means gives the identical 58-call crash, and reached improves 33 -> 36. The infinite sweep was HIDING that crash
entries.evidence: Made bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER for any address >= XBOX_TOTAL_RAM instead of a successful 64KB FREE region. This is a DIFFERENT change from #30 (which kept returning SUCCESS and only altered extents), yet it reproduces #30's outcome almost exactly: kernel_calls 58 (vs 58), safe_stub 8 (vs 8), failed_icalls 2 (vs 2), same crash RVA 0xD247F0, heap_allocs 16 (vs 18). Two unrelated changes converging on one outcome means the extents/overflow candidates (a)(b)(c) in #30 are all IRRELEVANT - the only thing that matters is whether the sweep terminates. Measured on `reached`, the signal that still has resolution once kernel_calls saturates: distinct dispatch targets 33 -> 36, so the boot goes FURTHER, not less far. #30 was reverted on kernel_calls 4000 -> 58, but #33 established 4000 is a logging cap over 21.6M calls of one useless ordinal, so that comparison was meaningless and the revert was made on a bad signal. Rule #14 needs `reached` as its tiebreak, not kernel_calls. The newly visible crash triages cleanly: read at Xbox VA 0xFFFFFFFE in sub_001E8F30+0x180, called from sub_0020F209+0x1FB7 (the same engine allocator chain), with esi = 0xFFFFFFFE = -2 and eax/ecx/edx all NULL - a plain "ptr - 2" computed from a NULL that a failed allocation returned and nobody checked. ROOT CAUSE NOW VISIBLE, and it is neither #30's nor mine: the k_regions table reports ALL FOUR in-RAM regions as MEM_COMMIT, including the ~49MB heap span 0x00F80000..0x04000000 which is almost entirely unused. So we tell the scanner every byte of the 64MB is committed and nothing is free. It rejects all four, walks off the top of RAM, and there we hand it endless 64KB "free" granules. NEXT TEST: report the heap tail above the native allocator's high-water mark as one large bounded MEM_FREE region, so the scan finds real free memory on its first pass inside RAM and never leaves it. #30's candidate (a) noticed the heap-as-one-committed-region was suspicious but reasoned about it backwards.

entries.claim: Reporting the heap above the bump allocator's high-water mark as one large MEM_FREE region kills the infinite sweep and lets the engine grow its pool for the first time
entries.evidence: Added xbox_HeapHighWater() (exposes the previously-static g_heap_next in xbox_memory_layout.c) and split the k_regions table in bridge_NtQueryVirtualMemory: XBOX_HEAP_BASE..high_water stays MEM_COMMIT, high_water..XBOX_TOTAL_RAM becomes MEM_FREE with AllocationBase/Protect/Type all zeroed the way a real free region reports. Empty spans are skipped so the table stays valid when the high-water mark sits at either end. Measured, deterministic 2 of 2: kernel_calls 58 -> 65, heap_allocs 16 -> 20, safe_stub 8, failed_icalls 2, reached 36 -> 37 (33 on the old hanging build, so this is the best reached ever recorded). The 21.6M-call sweep is GONE - total NtQueryVirtualMemory calls for the whole boot is now FIVE per pass. The log shows the mechanism working exactly as intended: the scan walks the four committed regions, finds ~49MB FREE at 0x0108CA90, TAKES it, and on each subsequent pass the committed heap has grown - 1,100,432 -> 2,424,832 -> 3,739,648 bytes - with the free region shrinking to match (49,755,504 -> 48,431,104 -> 47,116,288). That is the engine's pool growing, which is the thing that has never once worked on this project. It also correctly reports base=0x00F80000 when queried at 0x011D0000 after the high-water mark moves past it. REMAINING WALL, unchanged by this and now the top item: same crash as ledger #34, read at Xbox VA 0xFFFFFFFE in sub_001E8F30+0x180 (recomp_0014.c ~line 1071), reached from sub_0020F209+0x1FB7. esi = 0xFFFFFFFE = -2 with eax/ecx/edx all NULL - a MEM16/32 read at `ptr - 2` off a NULL. So something downstream still returns NULL and the caller does not check it; that is a separate bug from pool growth and was hidden behind the sweep until now. Note a diagnostic left in place deliberately: a [QVMSWEEP] counter in the bridge logs every 4096th NtQueryVirtualMemory call with a backstep count. It cannot fire at five calls per boot, so it costs nothing and will shout immediately if the sweep ever returns.

entries.claim: The sub_001E8F30 crash is a NULL handler registry at 0x5BC53C, never written because its init ICALL target is 0 - the object field g508+0x30 is still zero when sub_001F6FD1 runs
entries.evidence: Deep-dived sub_001E8F30 and reconstructed the crash from the registers alone, then confirmed the cause with one probe. THE ARITHMETIC CLOSES EXACTLY. sub_001E8F30 is the engine's "ask every registered handler to free memory" pass, called by the allocator under pressure. It walks two registries: `ecx = MEM32(0x5BC53C); edx = MEM32(ecx); esi = MEM32(edx + edi*4)` then dereferences `eax = MEM32(esi)` at loc_001E8F54. At the crash ecx=0, edx=0, edi=7, esi=0xFFFFFFFE. So MEM32(0x5BC53C) is NULL, edx = MEM32(0) = 0, esi = MEM32(0 + 7*4) = MEM32(0x1C) = 0xFFFFFFFE (guest low-memory garbage), and MEM32(esi) faults at 0xFFFFFFFE. Every register matches; nothing is inferred. The loop count is likewise bogus - `edi = MEM32(eax+4)` with eax NULL reads MEM32(4). WHY 0x5BC53C IS NULL: it has exactly ONE real writer in the whole tree, recomp_0014.c:37356 in sub_001F6FD1, and that store is SKIPPED on failure - `if (TEST_Z(eax,eax)) goto sub_001F700B` at loc_001F6FF9 branches past it. The eax being tested comes from ICALL MEM32(edx + 0xCC) where edx = MEM32(MEM32(0x5BC508) + 0x30). PROBED AT loc_001F6FF9, fires exactly once per boot: alloc_ret=0x00000000 g538=0x00000000 g508=0x01086000 vtbl=0x00000000 slotCC=0x00000000. entries.claim: g508+0x30 IS filled, by sub_0021644B at loc_002164A7, but it stores NULL because esi is clobbered by the preceding indirect call through vtable+0x6C = sub_001EC120 - a callee-saved-register preservation bug

THE FILLER EXISTS and runs: recomp_seed.c loc_002164A7 does `eax = MEM32(0x5BC508); MEM32(eax + 0x30) = esi;` then immediately calls sub_001F6FB0 to build the registries. NEXT STEP: read sub_001EC120 and find why esi is not preserved - compare its push/pop pairs against the original x86 (faithful.py, and ReVa get-decompilation on 0x001EC120). entries.claim: esi is not "clobbered" by sub_001EC120 - the stack is 40 bytes too deep at its epilogue, so POP32 reads uninitialised stack (zero) instead of the saved esi. The leak is entirely under the vtable+0xCC call to sub_001EC5E0
entries.evidence: Refines ledger #37, which said sub_001EC120 "clobbers esi". It does not overwrite esi - it RESTORES IT FROM THE WRONG PLACE. faithful.py is clean on sub_001EC120 (35 insns, ratio 1.54, no missing labels, no stale flags), so this is not a dropped branch. Probed g_esp and esi at entry, at all four ICALL sites, and at the epilogue. Entry [ECIN] esp=0x00F7FF20 esi=0x01088A90. After the two prologue pushes esp should be 0x00F7FF18 and it is: [ESP1] 0x00F7FF18 (after ICALL vtbl+0xC0) and [ESP2] 0x00F7FF18 (after ICALL vtbl+0x7C) - both calls balance perfectly. Then [ESP3] 0x00F7FEEC after the ICALL through vtbl+0xCC. Expected there is 0x00F7FF14 (0x00F7FF18 less the deliberate `push edi`), so that ONE CALL loses 0x28 = 40 bytes. [ESP4] 0x00F7FEEC - the vtbl+0xFC call adds nothing. At the epilogue [ECOUT] esp=0x00F7FEF0 with MEM32(esp)=0x00000000 and MEM32(esp+4)=0x00000800, so `POP32(esp, esi)` reads a ZERO that was never pushed. THAT zero is the value that reaches MEM32(g508+0x30). The saved esi is still sitting untouched at 0x00F7FF18. edi is destroyed the same way: [TCC] read edi=0 after the +0xCC call where it held the vtable 0x003F4770, which makes the following ICALL MEM32(edi+0xFC) resolve to MEM32(0xFC)=0 - that is one of the run's 2 failed icalls, so the failed-icall count is a SYMPTOM of the leak, not an independent fault. THE LEAKING CALLEE IS sub_001EC5E0, captured before the call because edi is dead after it: [PRECC] esi=0x01088A90 vtbl=0x003F4770 slotCC=0x001EC5E0 slotFC=0x001EC750. That matches the 2026-08-05 note naming sub_001EC5E0 the manager's allocate thunk on vtbl 0x003F4770. sub_001EC5E0's own arithmetic looks RIGHT - it pushes 3 args plus the dummy return and ends `esp += 8; return; /* ret 4 */`, the same shape sub_001E8F30 uses correctly - so the 40 bytes are lost BELOW it, in the call through vtbl+0x1AC that descends into the fpo_leaf allocator chain sub_00211530 -> sub_0020F860 -> sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209, the family whose g_seh_ebp frame inheritance the project notes already flag as fragile. NEXT STEP: walk g_esp down that chain the same way (probe at each fragment entry and exit) to find the frame that does not restore it. SEPARATE LATENT BUG worth fixing regardless: RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE (recomp_types.h:609) does `g_esp = (saved_esp)` on every failure path, and at loc_001EC176 the callee-save `PUSH32(esp, edi)` is emitted INSIDE the icall block, after `_icall_esp` is captured. So had that call failed, the rewind would have discarded edi's saved slot and the later POP32 would misalign. It did not fire here because the target resolved, but any fragment with a callee-save push inside an icall block has the same hazard. Tree clean: all probes stripped, 65/2/20/8 deterministic 2 of 2.

entries.claim: The 40-byte leak is inside sub_0020F209, on the path to its THIRD tail-jump to sub_0020F0B2 (return site #3): esp is exactly 0x28 below entry there, and every frame above inherits that same deficit
entries.evidence: Walked g_esp down the whole chain with entry/exit probes, then re-ran with a SEPARATE counter per return site after discovering the first pass under-sampled (all 8 sites of sub_0020F209 shared one static with limit 3, so the balanced epilogue never printed - worth remembering as a probe-design trap). entries.claim: Do NOT fix the 40-byte leak as the next step: it lives inside the game's FATAL out-of-memory reporter, which ends in `goto self` by design. The real blocker is vtable+0x1B0 (sub_001EC9C0) still returning -1, so pool growth is STILL failing
entries.evidence: Chased ledger #39's 40 bytes to the exact instruction and found the fix is not worth making. LOCALISED FIRST: probed g_esp at every label in sub_0020F209 - it holds steady at 0x00F7FE44 through loc_0020F34A/F35A/F451/F45E/F467/F480/F491/F499 and drops to 0x00F7FE1C only at loc_0020F4A7, so the loss is entirely the ICALL through vtable+0x54. Inside sub_001E8DB0: [S:DB0] esp=0x00F7FE38 g5BBA14=0x00011A60 (non-zero, so it takes the CALL path, not the early exit - sub_001E8DCC never fires), [S:DB9] 0x00F7FE38, [S:DC6] 0x00F7FE04 - 0x34 = 52 bytes gone across an ICALL that pushed only 16. Arithmetic closes exactly: 0x00F7FE04 + 0xC + 0xC = 0x00F7FE1C, and 0x00F7FE44 - 0x00F7FE1C = 0x28 = the 40 bytes. WHAT THE CALLEE IS, and this is the point: global 0x5BBA14 holds 0x00011A60, registered through sub_001E8DE0 (a one-line cdecl setter). sub_00011A60 installs a full SEH frame (push -1, push scope table, push fs:[0], mov fs:[0] esp, sub esp 0xC = 24 bytes) and runs a chain sub_00011A60 -> sub_00011AAE -> sub_00011AB4 -> sub_00011B35 of paired sub_001F8250 / sub_001EB1B0 calls against format strings at 0x3C7054, 0x3C701C, 0x3C7000, 0x3C6FE4, 0x3C6FC8, 0x3C6FAC, 0x3C6F90, 0x3C6F8C. That is a formatted diagnostic dump. sub_00011B35 ends `loc_00011E33: goto loc_00011E33;` - an unconditional self-loop, the console fatal-error halt. It DOES have a real SEH teardown at loc_00011C3F (restores fs:[0] from esp+0x14, pops, `esp + 0x18`), so the lifting is not obviously wrong; the leak is somewhere in that long fragment chain. CONCLUSION: this is the engine's fatal OOM reporter and it is MEANT to never return. Repairing the stack there converts the current crash into a clean hang inside a fatal error handler. That is tidier but it is NOT progress toward boot, and it would cost real time in a chain of 8+ fragments. THE ACTUAL BLOCKER, proven by the same label trace with no extra run: sub_0020F209 reaches loc_0020F363 and later loc_0020F451, and the only way there is `loc_0020F35A: if (eax != 0xFFFFFFFF) goto loc_0020F555` NOT being taken - so the ICALL through vtable+0x1B0 (sub_001EC9C0, the manager asking the system for memory) returned -1. It is called twice and fails twice, then sub_001E8F30 is asked to free memory twice (attempts 0 and 1 via MEM32(esp+0x1C)), then at attempt >= 2 control goes to loc_0020F499 and the fatal reporter. So despite ledger #35 making the OS-level pool grow (committed heap 1.1MB -> 2.4MB -> 3.7MB) and xbox_HeapAlloc succeeding 20/20 with zero failures, the ENGINE's own growth path still reports failure. NEXT STEP: instrument sub_001EC9C0 / sub_001EC9D8 / sub_001F09D0 and find which return produces the -1 now that NtQueryVirtualMemory reports real free memory. That is upstream of everything else here. Tree clean: all probes stripped, 65/2/20/8 deterministic 2 of 2.

entries.claim: The -1 is NOT minted in sub_001EC9C0 or sub_001EC9D8: sub_001F09D0 gets a SUCCESSFUL allocation (edi=0x011D0000) and throws it away, because loc_001F0AC7 compares an out-parameter against the never-initialised global 0x5BC5D8 and both are ZERO, so it loops back. This UNREFUTES ledger #32.

Confirms ledger #31's chain on the current build. Four calls per boot, two per manager object, args alternating pointer/0 which matches sub_0020F209's two vtable+0x1B0 sites. INSIDE sub_001F09D0, four return sites tagged individually: every call exits via RET4 (loc_001F0B0F), whose body is `eax = edi` - so the return value IS edi, and there is no explicit -1 on that path. Calls 1-3 arrive at loc_001F0A91 with edi already 0xFFFFFFFF and take `if (edi == -1) goto loc_001F0B0F` straight out. CALL 4 IS THE INTERESTING ONE: [F:L_001F0A91] eax=0x011D0000 edi=0x011D0000 - the allocation SUCCEEDED, and 0x011D0000 is exactly where the heap high-water mark sat, so ledger #35's fix IS delivering real memory. edi then survives the ICALL through vtable+0xB4 intact ([AFTB4] edi=0x011D0000), and [ATB03] never fires, so the success branch at loc_001F0B03 is NOT taken. Control goes loc_001F0AB8 -> loc_001F0AC7, and there: [AC7] edi=0x011D0000 MEM(eax)=0x00000000 g5BC5D8=0x00000000 match=1. The branch `if (ecx == MEM32(0x5BC5D8)) goto loc_001F09E0` is TAKEN, the loop goes round again, and the good 0x011D0000 is discarded; the function later leaves with edi back at -1. THIS UNREFUTES LEDGER #32, which recorded loc_001F0AC7 as firing ZERO times. That was true when measured, but it was measured BEFORE the NtQueryVirtualMemory work (#33/#34/#35). On the current build the branch is live and it is the decisive one. Refutations expire when the code underneath them changes - worth remembering as a general caution about this ledger. MECHANISM: at loc_001F0AB8 the code passes `esp + 0x20` as an OUT-PARAMETER to vtable+0xB4, and that call returns a stack pointer (eax=0x00F7FDF4). loc_001F0AC7 then reads MEM32(eax) - the out-parameter the callee was supposed to fill - and compares it against MEM32(0x5BC5D8). Both are zero, so the test passes and the loop repeats. Ledger #31 predicted exactly this ("very likely testing against a sentinel that never gets its real value") and marked it NOT YET PROVEN; it is now proven. OPEN, and the next fork: either (a) the vtable+0xB4 callee should be filling that out-parameter with something non-zero and is not, or (b) 0x5BC5D8 should hold a non-zero sentinel. 0x5BC5D8's only writer is recomp_0017.c:2652 in sub_00239E50, which stores ZERO deliberately at init, so (a) is the more likely of the two and should be tested first - identify the vtable+0xB4 target and check whether it runs or is a stub. Tree clean: all probes stripped, 65/2/20/8 deterministic 2 of 2.

entries.claim: CORRECTION to #41: 0x5BC5D8 is NOT an uninitialised sentinel and the loop-back is NOT discarding a good allocation. It is the SUCCESS status code. The -1 comes from a SECOND allocation on the loop's next iteration
entries.evidence: Tested option (a) from #41 and it is REFUTED, and testing it also overturned #41's own reading of 0x5BC5D8. THE STATUS-CODE PAIR: sub_001F1660 (the vtable+0xB4 target, resolved statically from the vtable at 0x003EECB0+0xB4) loads `ebp = MEM32(0x5BC5D8)` at entry as its default result and overwrites it with `ebp = MEM32(0x46A728)` on EVERY failure path (loc_001F16D9, loc_001F1753, loc_001F1771), then writes ebp into the caller's out-parameter. sub_00239E50 sets 0x5BC5D8 = 0 and 0x46A728 = 1 on adjacent lines (recomp_0017.c:2652-2653). So they are a deliberate SUCCESS/FAILURE pair, both correctly initialised, and `if (out == MEM32(0x5BC5D8)) goto loc_001F09E0` reads as "if it succeeded, go round again". #41 called this "throwing away a successful allocation"; that is wrong - the loop-back IS the success path. Ledger #31's long-standing "0x5BC5D8 is a sentinel that never gets its real value" suspicion is now definitively dead. (a) IS ALSO REFUTED ON ITS OWN TERMS: sub_001F1660 runs and succeeds. Probed its State branch - [G:ENTRY] flag=1 -> [G:CSTATE] State=0x00001000, and [G:ENTRY] flag=0 -> [G:DSTATE] State=0x00001000. All three FAILURE probes fired ZERO times. The commit path only accepts MEM_COMMIT (skip) or MEM_RESERVE (commit) and would fail on the MEM_FREE 0x10000 our bridge now reports, but the ranges it queries are inside already-committed heap, so that never arises. My MEM_FREE theory was wrong. A SECOND THEORY OF MINE ALSO DIED: sub_001F09D0's loop head has `PUSH32(esp, ebp)` inside it, which looked like a per-iteration leak, but esp is identical on both iterations (0x00F7FDE4) - no drift. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS, measured with an iteration probe at loc_001F09E0 (5 iterations across 4 calls): on call 4 iteration 1, ebx_slot=0 so it takes loc_001F09ED, ICALLs vtable+0x70, and `edi = eax` yields 0x011D0000 - a genuine success at the heap high-water mark. loc_001F0AC7 confirms success and loops back. On iteration 2 ebx_slot is STILL 0, so it calls vtable+0x70 AGAIN and `edi = eax` OVERWRITES the good address with the new result, which is -1. loc_001F0A91 then sends it to loc_001F0B0F where `eax = edi` returns that -1. So the loop allocates repeatedly until one fails, and the failure is the return value by design. THE REAL QUESTION IS NOW NARROW: why does the SECOND vtable+0x70 call fail? Resolved that slot statically via ReVa read-memory at 0x003EED20 -> bytes 50 E8 1F 00 -> sub_001FE850. Its first gate is a 64MB-block test: `if ((MEM32(0x46A668) >> 26) > (MEM32(0x5BBAD0) >> 26)) return -1` - position block vs limit block, and our RAM ends at exactly 0x04000000, so a position at the top of the heap lands in block 1 while a limit inside RAM is block 0. NEXT STEP: probe MEM32(0x46A668) (position) and MEM32(0x5BBAD0) (limit) at sub_001FE850's entry and tag its exits. THIRD EXPIRED REFUTATION IN TWO DAYS: the 2026-08-05 note says "I probed sub_001FE850 and it NEVER FIRES". It fires now. Same lesson as #32 - a refutation is only valid against the build it was measured on. Tree clean: probes stripped, 65/2/20/8 deterministic 2 of 2.

entries.claim: ROOT CAUSE of the -1: no memory region is ever registered. sub_001FE670, the only writer of the min/max pair 0x46A668 / 0x5BBAD0, NEVER RUNS, so they stay at their identity values and sub_001FE850's 64MB-block gate rejects every allocation
entries.evidence: Probed both globals at sub_001FE850's entry as asked. IDENTICAL on all three calls: [P:IN] pos=0xFFFFFFFF limit=0x00000000 posblk=63 limblk=0 size=0x00140000 gate_fails=1, and [P:RETNEG1] fires all three times. [P:PASSED] and [P:SAMEBLK] fire ZERO times, so sub_001FE850 never gets past its first instruction group - every allocation through vtable+0x70 returns -1 immediately. THE VALUES ARE NOT GARBAGE, which is the key insight and the opposite of what they look like. 0x46A668 = 0xFFFFFFFF and 0x5BBAD0 = 0x00000000 are the IDENTITY VALUES OF A MIN/MAX PAIR. Their only writer is the tail of sub_001FE670 (recomp_0015.c:5131-5147): `if (edx >= MEM32(0x46A668)) skip; else MEM32(0x46A668) = edx` is a min update, and `if (eax <= MEM32(0x5BBAD0)) skip; else MEM32(0x5BBAD0) = eax` is a max update. +inf and -inf are exactly right for an empty set. So sub_001FE850's gate `(min >> 26) > (max >> 26)` is not a RAM-boundary check at all - it is "has any region been registered yet?", and 63 > 0 is the correct answer for NONE. THE REGISTRAR NEVER RUNS: probed sub_001FE670's entry, it fired ZERO times on a full boot. sub_001FE670 is the region registrar - it fills a table at 0x5BBB38, ICALLs vtable+0xAC per entry, calls sub_001F0D20, then updates the min/max. Nothing is ever added, so the engine believes it owns no memory whatsoever. CALL CHAIN UP, for whoever picks this up: sub_001FE670 is reached by FALL-THROUGH from sub_001FE5C0, which has one real caller sub_001FFCD0 (recomp_0015.c:7701) plus a fall-through from sub_001FE570. So the next question is why sub_001FFCD0 -> sub_001FE5C0 -> sub_001FE670 never executes - whether sub_001FFCD0 itself never runs, or runs and takes a branch that skips the registration. RECONCILES THE EARLIER MEASUREMENT: ledger #42 saw edi = 0x011D0000 on one iteration and called it a success through vtable+0x70. It was not - only 3 of the 5 loop iterations take the ebx==0 path to vtable+0x70 (the others go to vtable+0x6C), and all 3 of those fail here. The 0x011D0000 came from the vtable+0xA4 FALLBACK at loc_001F09FB/loc_001F0A06, which succeeds while the fast path is dead. So the engine is limping along on its fallback allocator and failing as soon as the fallback cannot serve a request. Tree clean: all probes stripped, 65/2/20/8 deterministic 2 of 2.

entries.claim: FIXED: a deferred-flag miscompile at 0x001F0AB2 was why no memory region was ever registered. The lifter re-tested `cmp ecx, eax` after `mov ecx, esi` clobbered ecx, so the branch to the region registrar never fired. Repairing it takes reached 37 -> 43
entries.evidence: Probed sub_001FFCD0 as asked: it fires ZERO times, and so does sub_001FE5C0. But that turned out to be a dead end by design - sub_001FE5C0 ends in `ret` and does NOT fall through into sub_001FE670, so the "caller" the deepdive listed was a fall-through guess, not a real edge. ReVa find-cross-references on 0x001FE670 returns ZERO references of any kind. The generated header says `Category: game_vtable` and recomp_dispatch.c:15084 registers it, so it is reached only indirectly. entries.claim: The sub_00205170 garbage read is a live C++ object being walked as a heap block: its first word is the manager VTABLE 0x003F4770, read as a block header. This is ledger #29's no-block-header caveat arriving one level up, in the engine's own free-list coalescer
entries.evidence: faithful.py is CLEAN on sub_00205170 this time (199 insns, ratio 1.16, no missing labels, no stale flags) - I ran it enabled after ledger #44's lesson about no_faithful hiding a real defect. So this is not a lifting bug. THE CODE: sub_00205170 is the free-list coalescer. It reads a block header at MEM32(esi), unpacks the same 19-bit size field seen in sub_0020F0B2, and at loc_00205276 does backward merging: `ecx = MEM32(esi - 4); esi = esi - ecx; ecx = MEM32(esi)` - step back over the previous block using a footer. That backward path is guarded by `if (LO8(ebx) & 1) skip`, a PREV_INUSE flag in bit 0 of the header. PROBED both points. Iteration 1: [BLKHDR] esi=0x011D0004 hdr=0x00000203 previnuse=1 - a SANE block (bit0 set, size field 0x203>>5 & 0x7FFFF = 16), and it correctly skips the backward merge. Iteration 2: [BLKHDR] esi=0x011CD000 hdr=0x003F4770 previnuse=0. THAT VALUE IS NOT A HEADER - 0x003F4770 is the manager object's VTABLE POINTER, the exact value probed repeatedly in ledgers #37/#41 as `vtbl=0x003F4770`, and 0x011CD000 is the manager `this` seen in [M:C0] of ledger #41. So the coalescer is walking a LIVE C++ OBJECT and reading its vtable pointer as a block header. Bit 0 of 0x003F4770 is clear, so previnuse reads as 0, so it takes the backward-merge path it should never have taken: [BACKMRG] esi=0x011CD000 footer=0x00000000 newesi=0x011CD000 - the footer is zero so esi does not move, then MEM32(esi) yields 0x3F4770, which is treated as the next header and the walk continues into unrelated memory until it dereferences 0xD8282444 and faults. WHY THE OBJECT IS THERE: xbox_HeapAlloc is a pure bump allocator that hands out consecutive regions with NO engine block header and no gaps. Both 0x011CD000 (the manager object) and 0x011D0000 (the region the engine's now-working growth obtained, measured as edi=0x011D0000 in ledger #42) come from it, back to back. The engine assumes its pool is a contiguous run of blocks it carved itself, so walking off the end of one lands directly in a neighbouring bump allocation owned by something else. Ledger #29 predicted exactly this when the CRT heap was replaced - "anything stepping back from a block to read one now finds unrelated memory" - and it has now surfaced one level up, in the engine's own allocator rather than the CRT's, because #44 made pool growth work for the first time. NOT YET DECIDED, and worth separating before touching anything: (a) give xbox_HeapAlloc real block headers/footers so neighbours are walkable, (b) pad or guard-page between bump allocations so a walk terminates instead of wandering, or (c) find out why a live object is on the free list at all - iteration 2's esi comes from `esi = MEM32(eax)` at loc_002051D0, a list read, so the list contents are the thing to probe first. (c) is the cheapest and is the honest next step; (a) and (b) are workarounds that would hide it. Tree clean: probes stripped, 60/2/20/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 43.

entries.claim: Option (c) answered: the deferred-free array is FINE. sub_00205170's cursor and end are read from stack slots that drift 12 bytes per iteration, because two undetected functions (sub_001E6C5B, sub_001E6CC9) were stubbed with a generic `g_esp += 4` that restores 4 where the real epilogue restores 16. Seeding sub_001E6CC9 took reached 43 -> 47
entries.evidence: Probed the list as asked and it is HEALTHY, which kills option (c) as originally framed: [L:POOL] pool=0x011CE000 word=0x0000004B count=9 start=0x011CE004 end=0x011CE020, and the entries walk cleanly - [L:SLOT] cursor=0x011CE004 entry=0x00000000, then cursor=0x011CE008 entry=0x011D0004 (a block with a valid header). Third iteration reads cursor=0x0001FA68 (an address in .text) and end=0x00000018 - both garbage, both simply the wrong slots. Measured the drift directly: [LOOPESP]/[AFT9330] give esp 0x00F7FE3C -> 0x00F7FE30 -> 0x00F7FE24 -> 0x00F7FE18, exactly 0xC = 12 bytes per pass. SOURCE OF THE 12: sub_001E6C10 (called twice per loop iteration) pushes esi and edi then tail-jumps out on two of its three exits. But sub_001E6C5B and sub_001E6CC9 were BOTH in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c as `void sub_XXX(void) { g_esp += 4; /* not detected */ }` - 4 restored where 16 is owed, a 12-byte deficit that matches the measurement exactly. Kept anyway because it replaces a wrong stub with the real 51-byte body and is strictly more faithful, and it is not a regression. sub_001E6CC9: THIS IS THE ONE - reached 43 -> 47 (best ever), kernel_calls 60 -> 65, heap_allocs 20 -> 21, failed_icalls 2 -> 3, and the crash CHANGES CATEGORY from an access violation at 0xD8282444 to an integer divide-by-zero, which means the coalescer now completes instead of walking into unrelated memory. NEW WALL: integer divide-by-zero at RVA 0xDAEB5D = sub_001FAB40+0x83D, with ecx=0 and edx=0 as the divisor and edi=0x01310000 (the heap high-water region). GENERAL LESSON, third instance today: a generic stub is not neutral. `g_esp += 4` is only correct for a plain `ret` with no callee-saved pushes; for anything else it silently corrupts the caller's stack frame, and the damage surfaces far away. Worth sweeping recomp_stubs_unresolved.c for stubs that are tail-jump targets of functions with register pushes.

entries.claim: The divide-by-zero is a real `div r8` at RVA 0xDAEB5D, but sub_001FAB40 - the only symbol within 0x900 of it - contains ZERO division statements in its generated C. The attribution and the source disagree and that must be resolved before chasing the divisor
entries.evidence: Deep-dived sub_001FAB40 and could NOT find the division. Recording this as inconclusive rather than guessing, because every cheap explanation has been checked and eliminated. WHAT IS SOLID: (1) The exception is genuinely EXCEPTION_INT_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO - main.c:779 prints ep->ContextRecord->Rip directly, so the RIP is not a stack-scan artefact. (2) The faulting instruction is real. Parsed the PE section table and read the bytes at file offset 0xDADF5D: `41 8B 0C 1C  FF C8  41 03 C0  81 C1 A8 00 00 00  49 F7 F0` - and 49 F7 F0 is `div r8`, a REX.W 64-bit UNSIGNED divide. Registers at fault: ecx=0 edx=0 eax=4 edi=0x01310000. (3) The build is not stale - exe 16:48:58, recomp_0014.c 16:32:27, its .obj 16:32:43. (4) The map attribution is not a near-miss: sub_001FAB40 sits at sec1:0x00DAE320 and is the ONLY symbol in the following 0x900 bytes, with the next public symbol (sub_001FAFF0) 0x2010 away. (5) faithful.py is CLEAN on sub_001FAB40 - 389 insns, ratio 1.18, no missing labels, no stale flags - and I ran it enabled, not skipped (ledger #44's lesson). WHAT CONTRADICTS IT: sub_001FAB40's generated C spans recomp_0014.c lines 45421..45980, bounded by the next `void sub_...(void)` definition rather than by a `^}` guess, and contains ZERO division or modulo statements after stripping comments line-preservingly. Verified the search itself is sound by running the same matcher over the whole gen tree: it finds 605 functions that DO divide, in forms like `eax = (uint32_t)((int32_t)(_dividend / (int32_t)ecx))` and `fp_top() = fp_top() / fp_st(1)`. So the matcher works and sub_001FAB40 genuinely has none. NOTE also that a REX.W 64-bit unsigned div does not correspond to any 32-bit guest DIV the lifter would emit - the generated forms are 32-bit - which hints the instruction may come from the RUNTIME rather than lifted game code. NEXT STEP, and do this before touching the divisor: disassemble forward from sub_001FAB40's entry at RVA 0xDAE320 to 0xDAEB5D and identify which C statement that div belongs to, or dump the .obj to see whether the compiler emitted it from a macro (MEM32/XBOX_TO_NATIVE/fp_* are the candidates worth checking). Until that is settled, any theory about why ecx/edx are zero is unfounded. Tree clean: no probes, 65/3/21/8 deterministic, reached 47.

entries.claim: RESOLVES #47: the divide-by-zero is `_dividend / (uint32_t)ebx` at recomp_0014.c:45275 in sub_001FA9E0 - NOT sub_001FAB40. The divisor is ebx = MEM32(pool + 0x7DC), a granularity field that is zero. The map mis-attributed it because sub_001FA9E0 has no public symbol of its own
entries.evidence: Disassembled the native body forward from RVA 0xDAE320 with capstone (487 instructions) and matched the faulting instruction's neighbourhood to generated C by idiom, which settles ledger #47's contradiction. THE INSTRUCTION STREAM at the fault: `add ecx,7 / and ecx,0xfffffff8 / sub eax,ecx / sub eax,[rbx+rbp] / mov ecx,[r12+rbx] / dec eax / add eax,r8d / add ecx,0xa8 / div r8`. THE MATCHING C, found by searching the whole gen tree for the 0xFFFFFFF8 rounding idiom within 15 lines of a division - recomp_0014.c:45268-45276 inside sub_001FA9E0: `ecx = ecx + 7; ecx = ecx & 0xFFFFFFF8u; eax = eax - ecx; eax = eax - esi; eax = eax + ebx + -1; edx = 0; { uint64_t _dividend = ((uint64_t)edx << 32) | eax; eax = (uint32_t)(_dividend / (uint32_t)ebx); edx = (uint32_t)(_dividend % (uint32_t)ebx); }`. Every instruction corresponds, and the `uint64_t _dividend` explains the REX.W prefix that #47 could not account for - the lifter builds a 64-bit dividend from edx:eax, so MSVC emits a 64-bit `div r8` rather than a 32-bit one. That was the detail that made the instruction look like it could not be lifted game code. THE DIVISOR IS ebx, LOADED AT recomp_0014.c:45252 AS `ebx = MEM32(ebp + 0x7DC)` where ebp is the pool - so pool+0x7DC is a block-size/granularity field and it is ZERO. The crash registers corroborate exactly: ebx=0, edx=0, eax=4, esi=0, edi=0x01310000. progress.json already listed +0x7DC on 2026-08-05 as one of the pool fields worth reading ("off the pool at MEM32(manager+0x70): +0x2C (cursor), +0x48 (sentinel), +0x7DC") but it was never actually read. MAP-ATTRIBUTION LESSON, and it cost most of #47: triage resolves an RVA to the nearest PRECEDING public symbol. sub_001FA9E0 has no public symbol at its own address, so its code resolved to sub_001FAB40+0x83D, and I then correctly established that sub_001FAB40's C contains no division - a true statement about the wrong function. The check that broke the deadlock was matching the DISASSEMBLY to the C by idiom rather than trusting the symbol. When a triage attribution and the source disagree, disassemble; do not assume the map is right just because the next symbol is far away. NEXT STEP: probe MEM32(pool + 0x7DC) at sub_001FA9E0's entry and find who is supposed to initialise it - the same pool object whose +0x2C/+0x48 are already known good. Tree clean, no probes, 65/3/21/8 deterministic, reached 47.

entries.claim: pool+0x7DC is set CORRECTLY (0x1000, twice). The divide-by-zero is that sub_001FA9E0 reads it off a STACK address, because it is an fpo_leaf that inherits ebp via g_seh_ebp and the lifter publishes g_seh_ebp on tail-jumps ONLY - never on the 1624 direct RECOMP_ABI_CALL sites
entries.evidence: Probed both ends as asked. THE WRITER IS FINE: sub_00204E03 does `ecx = MEM32(0x5BB9AC); edx = MEM32(ecx); ICALL MEM32(edx + 0x50); MEM32(ebp + 0x7DC) = eax` - it asks the global system allocator for its granularity through vtable+0x50 (= sub_001F0BE0, index 20 in the 0x003EECB0 vtable dump) and stores the result. Measured: [7DC:W1] writing 0x00001000 to pool 0x01089A90, then again to pool 0x011CE000. So the field is initialised to 0x1000 = 4096 on BOTH real pool objects. Nothing is missing and nobody forgot to set it. THE READER IS WHERE IT BREAKS: [7DC:READ] pool=0x011CE000 val=0x00001000 on the first call - correct, matches the writer. [7DC:READ] pool=0x00F7EAB8 val=0x00000000 on the second - and 0x00F7EAB8 is a STACK address (the guest stack is 0x00780000..0x00F80000), not a pool object at all. So sub_001FA9E0 divides by MEM32(stack + 0x7DC), which is zero. ROOT CAUSE, and it is architectural rather than a single bad value: sub_001FA9E0 is `fpo_leaf`, so its generated prologue is `ebp = g_seh_ebp; /* inherit caller's frame */`, and it uses ebp as a LIVE INBOUND POINTER to the pool (fields +0x2C, +0x7DC, +0x7FC). In the original x86 that works because ebp is a real register that simply keeps its value across a `call`. In the recompiler every function declares its own local `uint32_t ebp`, so the value does NOT flow; g_seh_ebp is the only bridge. Counted in recomp_0015.c: `g_seh_ebp = ebp` is published on 563 TAIL-JUMPS and on ZERO of the 1624 direct `RECOMP_ABI_CALL` sites. The caller here, sub_0020AA90 (named by the crash backtrace, call at recomp_0015.c:31548), holds the pool in its own ebp - it reads MEM32(ebp + 0x7C4) and MEM32(ebp + 0x7C8) on the two lines immediately before - but calls sub_001FA9E0 without publishing it. So the callee reads whatever g_seh_ebp was last left holding by some unrelated tail-jump, which this run is a stack address. NOTE ebp is the ONLY x86 register the lifter models as a per-function local; eax/ecx/edx/ebx/esi/edi are all C globals and flow across calls correctly. That asymmetry is the whole bug. DO NOT reflexively make ebp a global or publish it at all 1624 call sites - that is exactly the wide-scope change seed_missing_functions.py's own docstring warns about ("this project has been burned by wide-scope changes before (61 -> 44)"). The bounded options, in increasing risk: (a) publish g_seh_ebp before ABI_CALLs whose callee is fpo_leaf AND reads ebp without writing it first - a small, checkable set the lifter can identify; (b) hand-fix this one call site in sub_0020AA90 and measure; (c) make ebp global. Start with (b) to confirm the diagnosis cheaply, then (a). Tree clean: probes stripped, 65/3/21/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 47.

entries.claim: (b) applied and PROVEN to fix both known call sites - sub_001FA9E0's entry ebp is now correct on every entry - but the crash is unchanged, because a THIRD execution reaches the division with ebp=0 without appearing at the entry probe
entries.evidence: Hand-fixed both RECOMP_ABI_CALL sites that reach sub_001FA9E0 by inserting `g_seh_ebp = ebp;` immediately before the call - recomp_0015.c in sub_0020AA90 (loc_0020AD13) and in sub_0020A8E0 (loc_0020AA25). Both carry the `/* Manual fix (not in original x86): ... */` marker and are persisted (manual_edits 1056 -> 1058, fix count 25 -> 27). MEASURED ONE AT A TIME per the 2026-08-05 rule: sub_0020AA90 alone - no change, 65/3/21/8 identical. Adding sub_0020A8E0 - also no change. THE FIX IS NEVERTHELESS CORRECT AND PROVEN, which is the useful part: a recomp_where probe at sub_001FA9E0's entry now reports `ebp=011CE000 f7DC=00001000` on BOTH calls, resolving the caller as sub_0020A8E0+0x61A <- sub_001E8F30+0x85B <- sub_0020F209+0x1FB7. Before the fix the second entry read ebp=0x00F7EAB8, a stack address. So ledger #49's diagnosis of the g_seh_ebp publish gap was right and the repair works at those sites. WHY THE CRASH SURVIVES, and this is new: sub_001FA9E0 contains TWO divisions, not one - recomp_0014.c:45278 and 45316, both dividing by the same ebx loaded from MEM32(ebp + 0x7DC). I had only ever looked at the first. Probing both: execution 1 gives [DIV1] ebx=0x1000 ebp=0x011CE000 and [DIV2] ebx=0x1000 ebp=0x011CE000 - correct. A THIRD execution then hits DIV1 with ebx=0, ebp=0, f7DC=0. ebp is ZERO there, not a stack address, and f7DC=0 is simply MEM32(0 + 0x7DC) read out of the zeroed guest low memory. THE OPEN CONTRADICTION: that third execution does NOT appear at the entry probe, which recorded only two entries, both healthy. So either sub_001FA9E0 is being entered other than through loc_001FA9E0 (it is a fall-through target of sub_001FA6F0, and it is registered in recomp_dispatch so it can also be reached by ICALL), or ebp is clobbered between entry and the division by an intervening call - ebx and ebp are both C globals here, so any callee with a bad epilogue destroys them, exactly the class ledger #46 found. NEXT STEP: probe sub_001FA9E0's entry with a HIGHER recomp_where limit (the default truncated at 2) plus a counter, and probe ebp immediately before and after each call inside the function between entry and DIV1. That distinguishes "third entry from an unseen caller" from "ebp clobbered mid-function" in one run. Both manual fixes KEPT - they are strictly more faithful, demonstrably correct at their sites, and not a regression. Tree clean: probes stripped, 65/3/21/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 47.

entries.claim: CORRECTION to #49/#50: sub_001FA9E0 does NOT use inherited ebp - it overwrites it at recomp_0014.c:45254 with MEM32(this + 0x70). The g_seh_ebp theory was wrong and both (b) edits were no-ops, now reverted. The real cause is a SECOND manager object at 0x01310000 whose pool pointer is NULL
entries.evidence: Probed the entry with --limit 12 as asked, which settles it: the entry fires EXACTLY TWICE, never three times, while DIV1 fires three times. There is no third entry and no loop - a scan of the function for backward gotos finds ZERO. THE ACTUAL SHAPE, from reading recomp_0014.c:45244-45256: `PUSH ecx/ebx/ebp/esi/edi; edi = ecx; ebp = MEM32(edi + 0x70); ecx = MEM32(ebp + 0x2C); ebx = MEM32(ebp + 0x7DC)`. So the inbound parameter is ecx (thiscall, the MANAGER), ebp is immediately OVERWRITTEN with MEM32(this + 0x70) (the POOL), and ebx is the divisor read off that pool. The inherited ebp from g_seh_ebp is pushed and then discarded without ever being read. That makes ledger #49's premise - "sub_001FA9E0 uses ebp as a live inbound value" - FALSE, and explains cleanly why the (b) fix in #50 changed nothing: it was a no-op. It also explains the misleading earlier measurement: the entry probe read `ebp` BEFORE line 45254, so it was reporting the inherited value, not the one the division uses. Probing the right thing (ecx and MEM32(ecx+0x70)) gives the answer immediately: call #1 this=0x011CD000 pool=0x011CE000 f7DC=0x1000, call #2 this=0x01310000 pool=0x00000000 f7DC=0x00000000. BOTH from the same caller, sub_0020A8E0+0x61A. So the second call passes a DIFFERENT manager, 0x01310000, whose +0x70 pool pointer is NULL - the divisor is then MEM32(0 + 0x7DC) = 0 read out of zeroed guest low memory. 0x01310000 is exactly the bump allocator's high-water mark at that point (the log's last NtQueryVirtualMemory shows the committed heap ending at 0x01311000), so it is a FRESHLY ALLOCATED, NEVER CONSTRUCTED manager object - allocated but its pool pointer never filled in. BOTH (b) EDITS REVERTED (manual_edits 1058 -> 1056). They were harmless no-ops but carried an explanation now proven wrong, and on this project a wrong recorded rationale is worse than no edit - the whole method depends on trusting the ledger and the in-tree comments. Signals unchanged by the revert: 65/3/21/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 47. THE g_seh_ebp PUBLISH GAP ITSELF IS STILL REAL and still worth recording - ebp is the only register modelled as a per-function local, published on 563 tail-jumps and 0 of 1624 ABI_CALL sites in recomp_0015.c - it simply is not the cause of THIS bug. NEXT STEP: find who allocates the manager at 0x01310000 and why its +0x70 is never set. sub_0020A8E0 makes both calls, so probe it for where the second `this` comes from - most likely a newly created pool/manager pair where construction is skipped or fails.

entries.claim: There is NO second manager. sub_001FAB40 clobbers esi - a callee-saved register - so 0x01310000 is just whatever it left in the global. Measured directly: esi=0x011CD000 before the call, 0x01310000 after
entries.evidence: Probed sub_0020A8E0 as asked and walked inward until the clobber was cornered. STEP 1 - the manager arriving at sub_0020A8E0 is CORRECT on both entries: [A8E0IN] #1 and #2 both esi=011CD000 pool70=011CE000 ebp=011CE000, callers sub_001E8F30+0x85B <- sub_0020F209 <- sub_0020EFD0. sub_0020A8E0 never assigns esi itself (checked the whole body), and esi IS a C global in this recompiler, so it flows in from the caller and both flows are healthy. So the corruption happens INSIDE sub_0020A8E0, between its entry and its call to sub_001FA9E0 at loc_0020AA25. STEP 2 - ruled out the obvious suspect. loc_0020A974 contains a lifted `rep movsd`/`rep movsb` block that uses esi as the memcpy source and then restores it with `esi = MEM32(esp + 0x14)`, which looked like a frame-offset hazard. Probed both sides: it fires ZERO times. Not it. STEP 3 - the answer, one probe either side of the only call inside the loop: [PRE1FAB40] before sub_001FAB40 esi=011CD000, [POST1FAB40] after sub_001FAB40 esi=01310000. sub_001FAB40 DESTROYS esi. On x86 esi is callee-saved, so sub_0020A8E0 is entitled to keep it across that call; here the registers are C globals, so a callee that fails to restore one silently corrupts its caller. THIS REFUTES THE "UNCONSTRUCTED OBJECT" READING IN #51. 0x01310000 is not a freshly allocated manager whose pool pointer was never set - it is simply garbage left in the esi global, and it happens to sit at the bump allocator's high-water mark because that is what sub_001FAB40 was last working with. Nothing is missing its construction; there is a register-preservation bug. Same class as #38 (esp leak corrupting POP32 restores) and #46 (generic stubs restoring the wrong amount) - the third distinct instance of "callee-saved state is not preserved across a generated call". NOTE sub_001FAB40 is faithful-CLEAN (389 insns, ratio 1.18, no missing labels, no stale flags), so the defect is not a mis-lift of its own body - it is either an unbalanced push/pop within it or, more likely given #46, one of ITS callees returning without restoring. NEXT STEP: probe esi at sub_001FAB40's entry and at each of its return sites to find which path loses it, then walk into whichever callee is responsible. Tree clean: probes stripped, 65/3/21/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 47.

entries.claim: sub_001FAB40 loses esi because its BODY leaks 8 bytes, misaligning the epilogue POPs. Pinned to the sub_001F8350 call at loc_001FAD63; sub_001F8350 itself balances, so the leak is inside sub_001EB390 / sub_001EB3AC - a printf-family path called from many sites
entries.evidence: Probed esi at sub_001FAB40's entry and all 6 return sites with per-site tags. Only two fire: [FB:ENT] esi=0x011CD000 esp=0x00F7FDE0 and [FB:R4] esi=0x01310000 esp=0x00F7FDD8. Return site 4 (loc_001FADAE) DOES `POP32(esp, esi)`, so the pop is present - it simply read the wrong slot. The esp arithmetic proves why: entry 0x00F7FDE0, and after the full epilogue (4 pops plus `esp + 0x24`) it should be back at 0x00F7FDE0 but is 0x00F7FDD8, EIGHT BYTES LOW. Prologue (`esp - 0x24` plus 4 pushes = 52) and epilogue (4 pops plus 0x24 = 52) balance on paper, so the loss is in the body - the same shape as ledger #38. LOCATED IT by probing esp immediately after all 20 call sites in the function: esp holds steady at 0x00F7FDAC through C01, C02, C03 and C08 (x3), then C11 reads 0x00F7FD88 where 0x00F7FD90 was due - 8 short - and esi is ALREADY clobbered there, reading 0x00000004. C10 reads 0x00F7FDA4 but that is EXPECTED, not a leak: its probe lands before the `esp = esp + 8` cleanup of the sub_001E9AE0 call. Do not misread it. C11 IS THE `sub_001F8350` CALL at loc_001FAD63 - 7 args pushed (28 bytes) with the caller cleaning via `esp = esp + 0x1C`. sub_001F8350 ITSELF IS BALANCED: it pushes 3 args plus a dummy (16) and cleans `esp + 0xC` plus `esp += 4` (16). So the leak is one level deeper, in sub_001EB390, which does `eax = 0x1000; call sub_00341D40` - that is __chkstk allocating a 4KB buffer - then either `esp + 0x1000; ret` on the quiet path or tail-jumps to sub_001EB3AC. sub_001EB3AC calls sub_0034278E (a vsnprintf-shaped 4-arg call, cleaned with `esp + 0x10`), then ICALLs through the global function pointer at 0x46A3BC, then cleans `esp + 8`, `esp + 0x1000` and `esp += 4`. Both look balanced on paper too, so this needs measuring rather than reading - candidates are the __chkstk model in sub_00341D40, the sub_0034278E call, and the ICALL through 0x46A3BC (note RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE rewinds g_esp to a value captured BEFORE its two argument pushes, which on a failure path interacts badly with the following `esp = esp + 8`). WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE CURRENT WALL: sub_001F8350 is a printf-family entry point called from at least sub_0020EFD0, sub_0020F209 and sub_001FAB40 with format-string constants (0x3F4600, 0x3F4588, 0x3F4528, 0x3EFB60). An 8-byte leak per call corrupts EVERY caller's frame, so this one defect plausibly explains several unrelated-looking failures. NEXT STEP: probe esp at sub_001EB390's entry, after the chkstk call, at sub_001EB3AC's entry, after sub_0034278E, and after the 0x46A3BC ICALL. One run names the leaker. Tree clean: probes stripped, 65/3/21/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 47.

entries.claim: FIXED: sub_001F83D0's 7-entry jump table had NONE of its targets registered, so every RECOMP_ITAIL through it failed, stranding a pushed esi. Seeding the taken target sub_001F840B takes reached 47 -> 54 and kernel_calls 65 -> 82
entries.evidence: Walked the esp leak from ledger #53 to its end. sub_001F8350's printf path is sub_001F8350 -> sub_001EB390 -> sub_001EB3AC, and probing every boundary showed all three are BALANCED: [A_entry390] esp=0x00F7FD7C, [B_afterChkStk] 0x00F7ED7C (exactly -0x1000, so the __chkstk model in sub_00341D40 is correct), [D_entry3AC] 0x00F7ED7C, [E_after278E] 0x00F7ED6C then back to [F_beforeICall] 0x00F7ED7C. The loss is entirely at the ICALL through the global hook 0x46A3BC: [G_afterICall] esp=0x00F7ED6C, 4 bytes low, and esi destroyed to 0x00000004. Probed the hook: it holds 0x001F83D0. INSIDE sub_001F83D0: it does `PUSH32(esp, esi)` at entry, loads the switch index with `esi = MEM32(esp + 8)`, and dispatches via `RECOMP_ITAIL(MEM32(esi * 4 + 0x1F84AC))` - a 7-entry jump table. Its balanced exit at loc_001F843F does `POP32(esp, esi); esp += 4; ret`. Measured: [JT:entry] esp=0x00F7ED70 esi=0x011CD000 (esi is the caller's MANAGER, a global), [JT:gotIdx] esp=0x00F7ED6C idx=4, [JT:preITAIL] tgt=0x001F840B - and [JT:balancedExit] fires ZERO times. So the tail jump never lands and the POP never runs, which is exactly the 4-byte leak, and the esi the caller gets back is 0x00000004 - the SWITCH INDEX left in the global. That is why it looked like a plausible object pointer for two turns. ROOT CAUSE: read the table from Ghidra at 0x001F84AC - entries are 0x001F83EF, 0x001F83F6, 0x001F83FD, 0x001F8404, 0x001F840B, 0x001F8443, 0x001F844A - and NONE of the seven is defined or present in recomp_dispatch.c. The lifter emitted the switch cases as unreachable blocks inside sub_001F83D0 (visible as dead code after the ITAIL) but never registered them as dispatchable, so EVERY indirect tail jump through that table fails. FIX: seeded 0x001F840B, the index-4 target actually taken. Deterministic 2 of 2: reached 47 -> 54 (biggest single jump of the session), kernel_calls 65 -> 82, heap_allocs 21 -> 22, and the crash changes category from integer divide-by-zero back to an access violation - read at VA 0xFFFFFFFD in sub_00205170+0x6F3. NOTE 0x001F8443 and 0x001F844A were seeded first and changed NOTHING, because index 4 is the only one taken on this boot; they are kept as strictly-more-faithful and not regressions. THE REMAINING FOUR (0x001F83EF, 0x001F83F6, 0x001F83FD, 0x001F8404) ARE STILL UNREGISTERED and will fail identically the moment their index comes up - seed them one at a time when reached. GENERALISATION WORTH SWEEPING: any RECOMP_ITAIL through a jump table whose targets are absent from recomp_dispatch.c has this bug. That is a mechanical check over the whole tree.

entries.claim: TREE-WIDE: 265 of 272 jump tables have targets missing from recomp_dispatch.c - 2,651 unregistered targets in total. Essentially every switch statement in the game is broken the same way sub_001F83D0 was
entries.evidence: Generalised ledger #54 into a tree-wide sweep. Method: extract every jump-table dispatch site from gen/*.c - both `RECOMP_ITAIL(MEM32(reg * 4 + 0xBASE))` and the non-tail `uint32_t _jt = MEM32(reg * 4 + 0xBASE)` switch form - read each table straight out of game/default.xbe, and check every entry against the 26,785 addresses registered in recomp_dispatch.c. The script SELF-CHECKS its VA->offset arithmetic against the known table at 0x001F84AC and refuses to run if that read does not match ledger #54's values, so a wrong mapping cannot produce a plausible-looking list. RESULT: 272 jump-table sites, 265 of them have at least one unregistered target, 2,651 unregistered targets in total. So this is not a quirk of one function - the lifter emits switch cases as unreachable blocks inside their owning function and never registers them as dispatchable, so EVERY indirect jump through a table fails and lands on whatever the ITAIL fallback does. Each failure strands the owning function's pushes, which is how it surfaces: a stack leak and a clobbered callee-saved register, far from the switch. DELIBERATELY NOT MASS-SEEDING. 2,651 seeds in one step is exactly the wide-scope change seed_missing_functions.py's docstring warns about, and the 2026-08-05 entry records a 25x regression (1452 -> 56) from batch-adding 13 unverified fragments. These targets are better founded than those were - they are read from real jump tables, so they are certainly real instruction starts - but each seeded fragment still runs from its address to the owner's end, duplicating tails, which is the exact mechanism of that regression. WHAT I DID INSTEAD: finished the one table proven to be on the boot path. Seeded the remaining four entries of 0x001F84AC (0x001F83EF, 0x001F83F6, 0x001F83FD, 0x001F8404) after 0x001F840B from #54. Deterministic 2 of 2: 82/3/22/8, reached still 54, crash unchanged. Neutral as expected - index 4 is the only one taken on this boot - but they are strictly more faithful and pre-empt the same failure the moment another index comes up. STAGED PLAN for the rest, in order of value: (1) when a wall involves a switch, check its table first - this sweep makes that a lookup; (2) seed per-table for tables owned by functions already on the boot path, measuring per table; (3) only consider a bulk pass once a per-table pass has shown it is safe, and back up seed_list.json first (the 2026-08-05 entry is explicit that this is what made recovery cheap). The sweep script is at scratchpad/sweep_jumptables.py and is worth promoting into tools_data/ - it is title-agnostic and re-runnable after any regeneration.

entries.claim: The faithful sweep does NOT yield a backlog of deferred-flag bugs. Its 1094 findings are dominated by unlifted stubs, and its flag column produces false positives; the accurate detector reports ZERO remaining sites. The class is clean
entries.evidence: Ran `faithful --sweep 0` as planned: 30,002 functions checked, 1,094 with findings. THREE LAYERS OF INFLATION, peeled one at a time. (1) The ranking is by missing labels weighted 10x, and almost every top scorer lives in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c - sub_000C2145 with 170 "missing labels", sub_0006129A with 121, and so on. A stub has no labels because it was never lifted, so those rows re-report the missing-function class, not a miscompile. (2) Filtering to the flags column in LIFTED code only gives 835 functions - but those collapse to 329 DISTINCT sites, because heavily overlapping fragments report the same site repeatedly (sub_002106B0 and sub_00210710 both report the identical two entries). (3) Of those 329, re-checking each against the real file text rather than the body faithful was handed shows 34 already carry an `_sf` snapshot repair, leaving 295 claimed. THE 295 ARE FALSE POSITIVES. Hand-checked recomp_0000.c:2871, reported as "test esi, esi then pop esi" in sub_000125B0. The actual generated C is `esi = MEM32(eax + ecx * 4 + 4); (void)0; /* test esi, esi - flags set */; PUSH32(esp, edi); if (TEST_Z(esi, esi)) goto ...` - the intervening instruction PUSHES EDI and never touches esi. faithful matched a `pop esi` that occurs elsewhere in the original x86, not between the test and the branch. CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY by the project's own purpose-built pair: find_stale_flag_tests.py scans 15,234 deferred-flag sites and reports "sites whose tested register is clobbered: 0", and fix_stale_flags.py answers "nothing to fix - already applied, or the detector reports none". Those two work from the generated C, which is the thing that actually runs, so they cannot be fooled by instruction pairing across branches the way the disassembly-side check can. CONCLUSION: the deferred-flag class is CLEAN. The one real instance (0x001F0AB2, ledger #44, worth reached 37 -> 43) was found and fixed today, and faithful DID name it correctly - so the checker is still valuable per-function, where its output is read with the source in front of you. It is its SWEEP mode that should not be treated as a work queue. PRACTICAL UPSHOT, and the reason this is worth recording as a refutation rather than a note: without this check the obvious next move was to work through 295 "known bugs", every one of which would have cost a build, a run and a hand inspection to disprove. Use find_stale_flag_tests.py for this class, not the faithful sweep. Tree unchanged by this investigation: 82/3/22/8 deterministic, reached 54.

entries.claim: CORRECTION to #55: the jump-table problem is 75 tables / 608 targets, not 265 / 2,651. The _jt dispatch form is SAFE and must not be counted, and seeded functions register in recomp_manual.c not recomp_dispatch.c. Zero remain on the boot path - that work is DONE
entries.evidence: Went to seed the boot-path tables and found my own sweep was wrong in two ways, both of which inflated it. ERROR 1 - THE SAFE FORM WAS COUNTED. The lifter emits two shapes. The bare `RECOMP_ITAIL(MEM32(reg * 4 + 0xBASE))` is the broken one (ledger #54). The other is `{ uint32_t _jt = MEM32(reg * 4 + 0xBASE); if (_jt == 0x002164CDu) goto loc_002164CD; ... RECOMP_ITAIL(_jt); }` - every target resolved inline by an explicit goto, with the ITAIL only a fallback. That form is FINE. Verified by reading sub_0021624C's table 0x00216590, which my sweep had flagged as "8/8 missing" while the generated C resolves all six distinct targets by goto. Counting it took the site count from 83 to 272. ERROR 2 - THE WRONG REGISTRY WAS CHECKED. seed_missing_functions.py registers through `recomp_lookup_manual()` in src/recomp_manual.c as `if (xbox_va == 0x001F840Bu) return sub_001F840B;`, NOT in recomp_dispatch.c. My sweep only read the dispatch table, so it reported the seven targets I had already seeded as still missing. CORRECTED FIGURES: 83 bare-ITAIL sites, 75 tables with unregistered targets, 608 distinct targets. Ledger #55's "265 tables / 2,651 targets" is withdrawn. THE BOOT-PATH WORK IS ALREADY COMPLETE. Checked all 20 functions in the current crash backtrace and the chains confirmed executing this session against the corrected sweep: ZERO have an unregistered bare-ITAIL table. sub_001F83D0's table 0x001F84AC was the only one on the path and all seven of its targets are seeded (0x001F840B in #54, then 0x001F83EF/F6/FD, 0x001F8404, 0x001F8443, 0x001F844A). The two tables that looked like boot-path hits, in sub_0021624C and sub_0021644B, are both the safe _jt form. So there is nothing further to seed here right now - the remaining 608 targets are all in functions the boot does not currently reach, and will become relevant as it gets further. TOOL FIXED AND KEPT: tools_data/sweep_jumptables.py now matches only the bare form, unions recomp_dispatch.c with recomp_manual.c, takes --func to check one function, and documents both mistakes in its header so they are not repeated. Re-run it after any regeneration or whenever a new wall involves a switch. Signals unchanged throughout: 82/3/22/8 deterministic, reached 54.

entries.claim: The 0xFFFFFFFD crash is in sub_002053F0, NOT sub_00205170 - triage mis-attributed it again. Also seeded sub_001ECAD0, a newly-reached missing function: reached 54 -> 55, failed icalls 3 -> 2
entries.evidence: TWO RESULTS, one a fix and one a correction. THE SEED: the failed-icall list changed after the jump-table fix (#54) from the usual 0x1/0x0 garbage to include 0x001ECAD0, a real-looking .text address - a sign we now reach code that calls it. sub_001ECAD0 appears NOWHERE in the tree: not lifted, not in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c, not referenced by any generated line, so it is reached purely through a function pointer. Seeded it (17 bytes, 0x001ECAD0-0x001ECAE1). Deterministic 2 of 2: reached 54 -> 55, failed_icalls 3 -> 2, kernel_calls and heap_allocs unchanged at 82 and 22. A small but real gain, and it confirms the pattern that a failed icall to a plausible .text address is a genuinely missing function worth seeding. It did NOT move the crash, so it is not the cause of this wall. THE CORRECTION, and this is the more important half: triage reports the crash as sub_00205170+0x6F3, but resolving RVA 0xDFC7B3 against the linker map puts it inside sub_002053F0, which spans 0xDFBD00-0xDFC820. The symbols either side are sub_002053CC at 0xDFBC60 and sub_0020563B at 0xDFC820, so the attribution is unambiguous. triage is using a symbol source that lacks sub_002053F0 (seeded_functions.json rather than the linker map) and therefore falls back to the nearest name it does know. THIS IS THE SECOND TIME TODAY - ledger #48 lost a full turn to exactly this, when a divide was attributed to sub_001FAB40 while the code belonged to sub_001FA9E0. The lesson from #48 should have been applied here immediately: when chasing a crash, resolve the RVA against build/*.map yourself before deep-diving whatever triage names. CONSEQUENCE: ledgers #45 and #46 deep-dived sub_00205170 for the EARLIER crashes at +0x5EA and 0xD8282444 and their findings about the coalescer stand on their own probe evidence, but the CURRENT wall was never in that function. sub_002053F0 is fresh ground - faithful is CLEAN on it (149 insns, ratio 1.28, no missing labels, no stale flags), it has no ledger history, its only caller is a fall-through from sub_002053CC, and it reads globals 0x5BC508 and 0x5BC5D8 with one ICALL through MEM32(edi + 0x98). STILL OPEN: which read produces 0xFFFFFFFD. Registers are eax=5 ebx=0x2F000000 ecx=0 edx=0 edi=4 esi=1. The function has NO reads with a negative displacement, and its only two reads off the zero registers are MEM32(edx + 0x30) and MEM32(ecx + 0xC0), which would fault at 0x30 and 0xC0, not at -3. So the faulting address is computed, and the honest next step is to disassemble sub_002053F0 forward from 0xDFBD00 to the fault - the technique that cracked #48 - rather than guess from the register dump. Tree clean: no probes, 82/2/22/8 deterministic 2 of 2, reached 55.

entries.claim: CORRECTION to my own #58: triage was RIGHT - the crash IS sub_00205170+0x6F3. I mis-parsed the linker map, reading the section-relative column as an RVA. The faulting instruction is the backward-coalescing footer read MEM32(esi + -4) with esi = 1
entries.evidence: MY #58 CORRECTION WAS ITSELF WRONG AND MUST NOT BE ACTED ON. The MSVC map has three address columns per row: `0001:00dfbd00  sub_002053F0  0000000140dfcd00 f  recomp_0015.c.obj`. The first is SECTION-RELATIVE, the third is Rva+Base with image base 0x140000000. I parsed the first as an RVA, which is off by the section VA, and that shifted every lookup. Re-resolved with the correct column (62,972 symbols): fault RVA 0xDFC7B3 -> sub_00205170 + 0x6F3, symbol at 0xDFC0C0. That is EXACTLY what triage said. sub_002053F0 is at 0xDFCD00, well past the fault. RE-CHECKED #48 THE SAME WAY, because it made the mirror-image claim: RVA 0xDAEB5D -> sub_001FA9E0 + 0x15D (symbol 0xDAEA00), while sub_001FAB40 sits at 0xDAF3A0. So #48's CONCLUSION was right - the divide really is in sub_001FA9E0, which idiom-matching had already established - but triage was genuinely wrong there while being right here. So triage is not reliably wrong; it is inconsistent. The durable rule is simply: resolve against the Rva+Base column yourself, which is authoritative either way. THE ACTUAL ANSWER, obtained by disassembling from the correct base 0xDFC0C0 (435 instructions, target on a clean boundary): 0x00DFC7B0 `lea ecx, [rdx - 4]` then 0x00DFC7B3 `mov edx, dword ptr [rcx + rax]` where rax holds the guest memory base loaded from [rip + 0x9be610]. So the faulting expression is MEM32(guest_reg - 4) and the guest register is 1, giving 1 - 4 = 0xFFFFFFFD exactly as reported. In the generated C that is `ecx = MEM32(esi + -4)` at loc_00205276 - the BACKWARD-COALESCING FOOTER READ, corroborated by deepdive's field list for sub_00205170 which shows esi with a -0x4 read and nothing else negative. SO WE ARE BACK IN THE COALESCER of ledgers #45/#46, one layer on: the walk now reaches loc_00205276 with esi = 1 instead of a block pointer, reads the previous block's footer at esi-4, and faults. Previously the bad value was a vtable pointer (#45) and then the walk was fixed by seeding (#46); now it is the small integer 1, which is the same signature as the switch index 4 that ledger #54 traced to a stranded jump-table push. NEXT STEP: probe esi at loc_002051D0 and loc_00205276 to see where the 1 enters the walk, and check whether it arrives from the deferred-free array or from a register clobbered across one of the loop's calls - both have precedent today. Tree clean: no probes, 82/2/22/8 deterministic, reached 55.

entries.claim: The 0xFFFFFFFD crash is an ALIASING bug: sub_00211280 decrements a refcount at MEM32(obj + 4) where obj = MEM32(esi + 0xB0) resolves to the POOL 0x011CE000, and pool+4 is simultaneously the first slot of the deferred-free array sub_00205170 walks. The refcount value 1 is then read as a block pointer
entries.evidence: Traced the fault end to end. THE FAULTING INSTRUCTION, from disassembling sub_00205170 at its true base 0xDFC0C0: `0x00DFC7B0 lea ecx, [rdx - 4]` then `0x00DFC7B3 mov edx, dword ptr [rcx + rax]` with rax the guest base - i.e. the generated `ecx = MEM32(esi + -4)` at loc_00205276, the backward-coalescing footer read, with esi = 1 giving MEM32(0xFFFFFFFD). WHERE THE 1 COMES FROM, probed at three points in the walk with a limit high enough not to truncate (the first attempt capped at 12 and hid it): the deferred-free array walks cleanly for several passes - cursor 0x011CE004 through 0x011CE020 with entries null except a valid block 0x011D0004 at 0x011CE008 - and then on a later pass `[W:LIST] cursor=0x011CE004 entry=0x00000001`. The SLOT ITSELF changed from 0 to 1 between passes. Confirmed downstream: `[W:HDR] esi=0x00000001 hdr=0x2F000000`, and LO8(0x2F000000) = 0 so the PREV_INUSE bit is clear and the code takes the backward-merge path exactly as in #45. hdr also matches ebx=0x2F000000 in the crash dump. THE WRITER, from a write-watch on 0x011CE004: RIP RVA 0xE4D125 = sub_00211280 + 0x365 (resolved with the Rva+Base column per #59). sub_00211280 is faithful-CLEAN (118 insns, ratio 1.23). Its two writes to +4 are the same idiom: `ecx = MEM32(esi + 0xB0); if (ecx == ebx) skip; edx = MEM32(ecx + 4); edx--; MEM32(ecx + 4) = edx; if (eax & 0x7FFFFF) skip;` - a REFERENCE-COUNT DECREMENT with the same 0x7FFFFF mask seen in sub_00011B35. So the value 1 is a refcount, not a pointer. THE CONFLICT: sub_00211280 treats MEM32(pool + 4) as a refcount field on the object at MEM32(esi + 0xB0), while sub_00205170 treats MEM32(pool + 4) as the FIRST SLOT of the deferred-free array - and #46 verified that array reading works, since slot pool+8 legitimately held the valid block 0x011D0004. Both cannot be right about the same four bytes. NOT YET PROVEN, and this is the fork: either MEM32(esi + 0xB0) wrongly holds the pool pointer when it should point at some refcounted object, or the array base is off by one slot. The cheap decisive test is to probe esi and MEM32(esi + 0xB0) at loc_0021133E and loc_00211369 and see whether that field is meant to be the pool at all - if it is a stale or mis-assigned pointer, the aliasing is the bug; if it legitimately IS the pool, then the pool genuinely carries a refcount at +4 and sub_00205170's array must start at +8. Tree clean: probes stripped, 82/2/22/8 deterministic, reached 55.

entries.claim: The current wall is sub_00205170+0x682 (fault 0xB0348CB9), NOT the +0x6F3 / 0xFFFFFFFD read that ledger #60 analysed. Same function, 0x71 apart, different read. Re-baseline before acting on #60
entries.evidence: Checked determinism after noticing the possibility tool's baseline crash did not match my earlier measurement. Per-build determinism is FINE: 4 of 4 runs give exactly RVA=0xDFC742, all four counters identical, verdict deterministic. Tree integrity also verified - zero probe lines left in gen/, all four of today's seeds still registered in recomp_manual.c (sub_001F840B, sub_001ECAD0, sub_001E6CC9, sub_001E6C5B), and the deferred-flag manual fix still present in recomp_0014.c. So this is not a dirty tree and not run-to-run noise. BUT THE WALL MOVED between measurements. Resolved both addresses against the Rva+Base column: 0xDFC7B3 = sub_00205170 + 0x6F3 and 0xDFC742 = sub_00205170 + 0x682. Same function, 0x71 apart, but the fault address differs completely - 0x10000FFFD (guest 0xFFFFFFFD, the esi-4 footer read with esi=1) versus 0xB0348CB9 (guest ~0xB0338CB9, wild garbage). Those are DIFFERENT reads in the same coalescer loop. I cannot cleanly attribute the shift. The +0x6F3 measurement was taken probe-free right after seeding sub_001ECAD0; the current one is probe-free too. Candidates: the possibility tool builds via build_compile.bat directly while the MCP build may take another path, or a probe/strip cycle changed layout - ledger #17 already refuted "probes are behaviourally free". Not worth chasing on its own; what matters is the consequence. CONSEQUENCE, and this is why it is recorded rather than shrugged off: ledger #60's whole analysis - the refcount/array aliasing at pool+4, the write-watch, the sub_00211280 attribution - was of the +0x6F3 read. It is sound for THAT read but is NOT established as the cause of the wall standing in front of us now. The possibility run is still informative: variant A (suppress the refcount store to the pool) MOVED the crash while variant B (shift the array base to +8) was completely inert, so the aliasing is real and the array base is not the problem. But neither improved reached, and A merely moved the crash to the +0x6F3 read - i.e. A converts the current wall into the previously-analysed one. NEXT STEP: re-triage the CURRENT crash at +0x682 from scratch - resolve the faulting instruction by disassembling from sub_00205170's true base and read what it dereferences - before spending anything further on #60. Two turns were already lost today to acting on a mis-identified location.

entries.claim: RESOLVES #61: +0x682 and +0x6F3 are ONE bug, not two. Both consume esi = 1 from the corrupted deferred-free slot at pool+4; which garbage read faults first depends only on code layout. Ledger #60's analysis DOES apply to the live wall
entries.evidence: Re-triaged +0x682 from scratch as planned. THE FAULTING INSTRUCTION, disassembled from sub_00205170's true base 0xDFC0C0 (406 insns, clean boundary): `0x00DFC733 mov rax, [rip + 0x9be686]` loads the guest memory base, `0x00DFC73E add ecx, [r12 + r14]` computes block + size, then `0x00DFC742 mov edx, [rcx + rax]` faults - and the next instructions are `mov eax, edx; shr eax, 5`, the 19-bit size unpack seen throughout this allocator. So +0x682 is the FORWARD walk `edx = MEM32(edi + esi)`: step to the next block and read its header. +0x6F3, analysed in #60, is the BACKWARD merge `ecx = MEM32(esi + -4)`. Different reads, same loop. THEY SHARE ONE CAUSE. Probed the walk with a limit high enough not to truncate: [S:LIST] cursor=0x011CE004 entry=0x00000001, then [S:BLK] esi=0x00000001 hdr=0x2F000000, then [S:NEXT] esi=0x00000001 ebx=0x2F000000. That is the SAME corrupted array slot #60 traced to sub_00211280's refcount decrement, and the same header 0x2F000000 read out of guest low memory at MEM32(1). With esi = 1 the unpacked size is garbage, so `edi + esi` is garbage and the forward read faults; on a different layout the backward read faults first instead. CONFIRMED BY THE FLIP: stripping the probes moved the crash back from 0xDFC742 (+0x682) to 0xDFC7B3 (+0x6F3), deterministic 2 of 2 either way. The wall did not change between measurements - the same corruption simply exits through whichever garbage read the code layout puts first. That fully explains the "wall moved" puzzle in #61, which is now closed. entries.claim: ROOT CAUSE REACHED: the `this` is an ALLOCATION RETURN VALUE. sub_00222628 calls the engine allocator sub_001F7E00 for 0x10 bytes and gets back 0x011CE000 - the live pool - then constructs a C++ object on it. The engine allocator is handing out memory it is still using
